results.result: TLR ligand-stimulated supernatants from THP-1 cells and PBMCs inhibit SARS-CoV-2 spike-induced cell-cell fusion and reduce viral markers during authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection. The inhibitory effect is mediated by secreted factors, not by TLR ligands alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C15 provide convergent evidence from multiple assays (bioluminescence, S2' cleavage, syncytia area) and cell types (HEK293T-ACE2, Caco-2) showing that TLR-stimulated supernatants inhibit fusion. Control experiments (C12) demonstrate TLR ligands alone have no effect, confirming the role of secreted factors. The data are internally consistent across different readouts.

results.result: IL-1α and IL-1β are identified as the key cytokines secreted by TLR-stimulated innate immune cells that inhibit SARS-CoV-2-induced cell-cell fusion. IL-1β secretion depends on TLR2 and downstream TAK1/IKKβ signaling, and the inhibitory effect is blocked by IL-1RA.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C27 establish IL-1β as the active factor through cytokine screening (C16-C18), dose-response (C17-C18), authentic virus validation (C21-C22), ELISA confirmation (C23), and mechanistic validation using IL-1RA (C24), TLR2 knockout (C25-C26), and pathway inhibitors (C27). The evidence is comprehensive and internally consistent.

results.result: IL-1β inhibits cell-cell fusion induced by multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants and other beta-coronaviruses (SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV), acting on both spike-expressing and ACE2-expressing cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 demonstrate broad antiviral activity across viral variants (Alpha, Beta, Delta, Omicron) and related coronaviruses. The pre-treatment experiments (C28) show IL-1β acts on both donor and acceptor cells. The data support a general mechanism rather than variant-specific effects.

results.result: IL-1β inhibits SARS-CoV-2-induced cell-cell fusion through an IL-1R1-MyD88-IRAK-TRAF6 signaling pathway that is independent of the canonical TAK1-IKKβ-NF-κB cascade.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C40 systematically dissect the signaling pathway using IL-1RA (C31), genetic knockouts (C32, C34), and pharmacological inhibitors (C33, C37). The independence from TAK1-IKKβ-NF-κB (C36-C39) is demonstrated through multiple approaches. Validation in authentic virus-infected cells (C40) strengthens the findings. The pathway delineation is rigorous.

results.result: IL-1β activates RhoA signaling in a MyD88/TRAF6-dependent manner, leading to enrichment of active RhoA and actin bundles at cell-cell junctions. This actin reorganization prevents membrane fusion during syncytia formation, and the effect is reversed by ROCK inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48 provide mechanistic insight through RhoA pull-down assays (C41), live-cell imaging with GFP-AHPH biosensor (C42-C44), constitutively active RhoA experiments (C45), and F-actin visualization (C46-C47). The ROCK inhibitor rescue experiments (C48) provide strong causal evidence. The temporal dynamics and spatial localization data are compelling.

results.result: During authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection, IL-1β induces actin bundle formation at cell-cell junctions through RhoA/ROCK signaling, preventing syncytia formation. Constitutive RhoA activation mimics IL-1β effects, while ROCK inhibition abolishes them. IL-1β does not affect ACE2 or spike surface distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C60 validate the mechanism in authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection across multiple cell types (HEK293T-ACE2, Caco-2, Calu-3, primary human lung cells). The RhoA-CA gain-of-function (C53-C54) and Y-27632 loss-of-function (C58-C60) experiments provide strong causal evidence. Control experiments (C55-C57) rule out effects on receptor/ligand distribution.

results.result: In SARS-CoV-2-infected mice, IL-1β treatment reduces body weight loss, lung injury, viral N gene expression, and infected area in lung epithelium through induction of actin bundles. The protective effect is IL-1R-dependent and extends to multiple tissue types without causing toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C69 demonstrate in vivo efficacy through multiple readouts: clinical (C61-C63), molecular (C64), histological (C65), and mechanistic (C67). IL-1RA antagonism (C62) confirms receptor dependence. Toxicity assessment (C68) and ex vivo validation (C69) strengthen the findings. The data are comprehensive and internally consistent.

results.result: ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 abolishes the protective effects of IL-1β in SARS-CoV-2-infected mice, increasing body weight loss, lung injury, viral gene expression, and infected area by preventing actin bundle formation. This confirms that IL-1β acts through the RhoA/ROCK pathway in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76 provide in vivo validation of the RhoA/ROCK mechanism through pharmacological inhibition. The Y-27632 experiments reverse all protective effects of IL-1β (C70-C72), prevent actin bundle formation (C73), and abolish antiviral activity at multiple time points (C74-C75). The conclusion (C76) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Background claims establish the COVID-19 pandemic impact, viral evolution, syncytia formation in SARS-CoV-2 infection, its role in pathogenesis and immune evasion, and the context of impaired interferon responses in severe COVID-19.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims set the scientific context for the study but do not represent novel findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: Summary claims from the abstract stating that IL-1β inhibits syncytia formation through non-canonical IL-1R signaling that activates RhoA/ROCK and drives actin bundle enrichment, with in vivo validation in mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are high-level summary statements that accurately reflect the detailed experimental findings presented in other claim groups. These abstract-level claims are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Discussion claims contextualizing the findings within existing literature on IL-1β in COVID-19, vaccine responses, MyD88/IRAK4 deficiency, cell fusion biology, and corticosteroid effects on viral clearance.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C95 provide literature context supported by appropriate citations. These discussion points interpret the study's findings in light of existing knowledge but do not represent novel experimental findings. The citations appear appropriate, though some claims involve speculation (C89, C91).

results.result: TLR ligand-stimulated supernatants from THP-1 cells and PBMCs significantly reduced SARS-CoV-2 spike-induced cell-cell fusion, S2' cleavage, and syncytia formation in both spike-based fusion assays and authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection models. TLR ligands alone had no effect, demonstrating that soluble factors secreted by activated innate immune cells mediate this inhibition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, with one stating 'they demonstrate that soluble factors in the supernatants of TLR stimulated THP1 cells reduce fusion events' and another noting the authors 'used a cell-cell fusion assay developed previously to identify IL-1α/β as the cytokines that inhibit syncytia formation.' The bioluminescence assay is praised as 'a robust quantitative method.'

results.result: Through cytokine screening, IL-1α and IL-1β were identified as the key cytokines responsible for inhibiting SARS-CoV-2 spike-induced syncytia formation. Both cytokines significantly reduced bioluminescence signal, S2' cleavage, and syncytia area in spike-based fusion assays and authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection, with no synergistic effect when combined.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm this identification, with one stating 'they convincingly demonstrate that recombinant IL-1 cytokines are sufficient to reduce cell-to-cell fusion mediated by the S protein' and another noting 'they used a cell-cell fusion assay developed previously to identify IL-1α/β as the cytokines that inhibit syncytia formation.' The study is described as identifying 'a new mechanism by which IL-1 cytokines can limit virus infection.'

results.result: IL-1RA treatment blocked the inhibitory effect of TLR-stimulated supernatants on cell-cell fusion. TLR2 was essential for IL-1β secretion in response to TLR2 ligands, and TLR2 knockout or TAK1/IKKβ inhibition in THP-1 cells prevented IL-1β secretion and eliminated the inhibitory effect on fusion.
results.evaluation: These findings are part of the mechanistic pathway that reviewers affirm. One reviewer notes the authors 'demonstrate that IL-1 cytokines are (not surprisingly) upregulated by TLR treatment in THP1 cells' using 'qRT-PCR and ELISA.' The pathway from TLR activation to IL-1β secretion is accepted as part of the overall mechanism.

results.result: IL-1β inhibited spike-induced cell-cell fusion across different SARS-CoV-2 variants (Alpha, Beta, Delta, Omicron) and other coronaviruses (SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV). Pre-treatment of either spike-expressing or ACE2-expressing cells with IL-1β reduced fusion, with additive effects when both cell types were pre-treated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise this breadth of testing. One states 'the authors tested IL-1 mediated inhibition of fusion induced by many different coronavirus S proteins and several SARS-CoV-2 strains' as a strength. Another notes 'diverse cell types and in vivo models were used, and consistent results were shown across diverse models.'

results.result: IL-1β inhibits SARS-CoV-2 spike-induced cell-cell fusion through the IL-1R1-MyD88-IRAK-TRAF6 pathway. Blocking any of these components (IL-1RA, MyD88 knockout, IRAK1/4 inhibitor, or TRAF6 knockout) eliminated IL-1β's inhibitory effect on fusion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirm this mechanistic finding. One states 'they demonstrate that components of the myddosome (MYD88, IRAK1/4, and TRAF6) are required for fusion inhibition' and another notes 'they found that IL-1 prevents cell-cell fusion through MyD88/IRAK/TRAF6 but not TAK1/IKK/NF-κB.' This is described as revealing 'the inhibition of cell fusion did not require a transcriptional response and was mediated by IL-1R proximal signaling effectors.'

results.result: IL-1β inhibits SARS-CoV-2 spike-induced cell-cell fusion independent of the TAK1-IKKβ-NF-κB signaling cascade. IL-1β retained its inhibitory effect in TAK1 knockout cells, in the presence of IKKβ inhibitor, and after knockout of NF-κB pathway genes, demonstrating a non-canonical signaling mechanism.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. One states 'they demonstrate that components of the myddosome (MYD88, IRAK1/4, and TRAF6) are required for fusion inhibition, but that downstream canonical signaling (i.e., TAK1 and NFKB activation) is not required.' This is highlighted as revealing 'the inhibition of cell fusion did not require a transcriptional response.'

results.result: IL-1β activates RhoA signaling through a non-canonical IL-1 receptor-dependent pathway requiring MyD88 and TRAF6. IL-1β treatment caused RhoA activation and redistribution to cell-cell junctions, where it accumulated over time to prevent fusion, contrasting with the peripheral localization observed without IL-1β treatment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirm this mechanism. One states 'the authors identified RhoA/ROCK activation by IL-1 as the basis for this inhibition of cell fusion. By visualizing a RhoA biosensor and actin, they found a redistribution of RhoA to the cell periphery and cell-cell junctions after IL-1 stimulation.' Another notes this is 'a non-canonical RhoA/ROCK signaling pathway' and describes it as 'convincing evidence.'

results.result: IL-1β drives the enrichment of actin bundles at cell-cell junctions through RhoA/ROCK activation, creating barriers that prevent membrane fusion. Constitutively active RhoA mimicked IL-1β's effect, while ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 prevented actin bundle formation and restored syncytia formation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this mechanism. One states IL-1β 'triggered the formation of actin bundles at cell-cell junctions, preventing fusion and syncytia formation. The authors confirmed this molecular mechanism by using constitutively active RhoA and an inhibitor of ROCK.' Another notes 'the authors demonstrate that expression of a constitutively active RhoA alone is sufficient to inhibit fusion and that chemical inhibition of Rock could reverse this inhibition.'

results.result: During authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection, RhoA (visualized by GFP-AHPH) and F-actin relocalized away from cell-cell junctions and to the periphery during syncytia formation. IL-1β treatment reversed this, causing RhoA and actin bundles to accumulate at cell-cell junctions, preventing fusion. Constitutively active RhoA mimicked this effect in infected cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings as part of the overall mechanism. One notes 'diverse cell types and in vivo models were used, and consistent results were shown across diverse models. These results were convincing and well-presented.' The consistency between spike-based and authentic infection models is implicitly accepted through the reviewers' overall positive assessment.

results.result: RhoA-CA and IL-1β treatment did not affect Spike protein binding to ACE2 or the distribution of ACE2 or Spike protein on the cell surface, indicating that the inhibition of fusion occurs through cytoskeletal rearrangement rather than receptor-ligand interaction.
results.evaluation: While not explicitly discussed by reviewers, this control experiment is implicitly accepted as part of the overall mechanism that reviewers describe as 'convincing' and 'well-presented.' The reviewers' acceptance of the RhoA/actin mechanism without questioning alternative explanations suggests these controls were adequate.

results.result: ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 promoted syncytia formation in a dose-dependent manner and abolished IL-1β's inhibitory effect on S2' cleavage, N protein levels, and actin bundle formation during authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection in multiple cell types including primary human lung cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding as confirming the RhoA/ROCK mechanism. One states 'the authors demonstrate that expression of a constitutively active RhoA alone is sufficient to inhibit fusion and that chemical inhibition of Rock could reverse this inhibition.' The use of the ROCK inhibitor is accepted as validating the pathway.

results.result: In vivo infection experiments in mice confirmed that IL-1β treatment significantly reduced body weight loss, pulmonary injury, viral N gene expression, and infected area in lung tissue during SARS-CoV-2 infection. IL-1β induced actin bundle formation at cell-cell junctions in infected lung epithelial cells, restricting syncytia formation and viral transmission. IL-1RA co-treatment abolished these protective effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirm these in vivo findings. One states 'in vivo infection experiments in mice confirmed that IL-1β significantly restricted SARS-CoV-2 spread in the lung epithelium' and notes 'the authors demonstrate that recombinant IL-1 can reduce viral burden and lung pathogenesis in a mouse model of infection.' Another states this 'suggests that this process may also function to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection in vivo.'

results.result: IL-1β treatment did not cause toxicity in uninfected mice (no changes in body weight, liver, or spleen weight) and conferred lasting protective effects, as tissue cells isolated from IL-1β-treated mice remained resistant to SARS-CoV-2 infection ex vivo.
results.evaluation: While not explicitly discussed, these safety and durability findings are implicitly accepted as part of the in vivo validation that reviewers describe positively. The reviewers' overall assessment of the in vivo work as 'convincing' suggests these supporting data were adequate.

results.result: Y-27632 treatment abolished IL-1β's protective effects in vivo, compromising prevention of weight loss, aggravating lung injury, increasing viral N gene expression and infected area, and preventing actin bundle formation. This confirmed that IL-1β prevents SARS-CoV-2 transmission through the RhoA/ROCK pathway in vivo.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this in vivo validation of the mechanism. One states 'use of a ROCK inhibitor in IL-1 treated mice restored the ability of SARS-CoV-2 to spread in the lung, suggesting that this inhibitory process functions in vivo' and another notes 'the authors demonstrate that recombinant IL-1 mediated inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 infection in mice is dependent on the RhoA/Rock pathway.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C9-C15. Both evaluations affirm that TLR-stimulated supernatants inhibit fusion through multiple assays (bioluminescence, S2' cleavage, syncytia area). Peer reviewers explicitly praise the bioluminescence assay as 'robust quantitative method' and confirm the finding that 'soluble factors in the supernatants of TLR stimulated THP1 cells reduce fusion events.'

Strong agreement on IL-1β identification (C16-C18, C20-C23). OpenEval covers additional mechanistic validation claims (C24-C27) that peer reviewers address separately in R3. Both evaluations affirm the identification of IL-1α/β as the cytokines inhibiting syncytia formation, with peer reviewers describing the evidence as 'convincing.'

Partial overlap on mechanistic validation (C24-C27). OpenEval groups these with broader IL-1β identification claims, while peer reviewers evaluate them separately as part of the TLR-to-IL-1β pathway. Both affirm the use of IL-1RA, TLR2 knockout, and pathway inhibitors, with peer reviewers noting qRT-PCR and ELISA validation.

Perfect agreement on claims C28-C30. Both evaluations affirm the broad antiviral activity across viral variants (Alpha, Beta, Delta, Omicron) and related coronaviruses. Peer reviewers explicitly praise this breadth as a strength, noting 'diverse cell types and in vivo models were used, and consistent results were shown.'

Strong agreement on MyD88/IRAK/TRAF6 pathway (C31-C35). OpenEval covers additional claims about TAK1-IKK-NF-κB independence (C36-C40) that peer reviewers address in R6. Both affirm the requirement for myddosome components using genetic knockouts and pharmacological inhibitors.

Strong agreement on TAK1-IKK-NF-κB independence (C36-C40). OpenEval groups these with broader signaling pathway claims (C31-C40), while peer reviewers evaluate them separately. Both explicitly affirm that 'downstream canonical signaling (i.e., TAK1 and NFKB activation) is not required' and that inhibition occurs without transcriptional response.

Strong agreement on RhoA activation mechanism (C41-C44). OpenEval covers additional F-actin and ROCK inhibitor claims (C45-C48) that peer reviewers address in R8. Both affirm RhoA redistribution to cell periphery and junctions using biosensor imaging, with peer reviewers describing this as 'convincing evidence' of a 'non-canonical RhoA/ROCK signaling pathway.'

Strong agreement on actin bundle formation and ROCK mechanism (C45-C48). OpenEval groups these with RhoA activation claims (C41-C48), while peer reviewers evaluate them separately. Both affirm that constitutively active RhoA is sufficient to inhibit fusion and that ROCK inhibition reverses this effect.

Strong agreement on authentic virus validation (C49-C54). OpenEval covers additional control and inhibitor experiments (C55-C60) that peer reviewers address separately. Both affirm validation across multiple cell types with consistent results, with peer reviewers noting 'diverse cell types and in vivo models were used.'

Agreement on control experiments (C55-C57). OpenEval groups these with broader authentic virus validation (C49-C60), while peer reviewers implicitly accept these controls as part of the overall mechanism described as 'convincing and well-presented.' Both evaluations support that the mechanism does not involve altered receptor/ligand distribution.

Agreement on ROCK inhibitor validation in authentic infection (C58-C60). OpenEval groups these with broader authentic virus validation (C49-C60), while peer reviewers evaluate them separately. Both affirm that ROCK inhibition reverses the fusion inhibition, confirming the RhoA/ROCK pathway.

Strong agreement on in vivo efficacy (C61-C67). OpenEval includes additional claims (C68-C69) that peer reviewers address in R13. Both strongly affirm that IL-1β restricts SARS-CoV-2 spread in mouse lungs with reduced viral burden and pathogenesis, with peer reviewers describing the evidence as 'convincing.'

Agreement on safety and durability (C68-C69). OpenEval groups these with broader in vivo efficacy claims (C61-C69), while peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of the overall in vivo validation. Both evaluations support the safety and sustained effect of IL-1β treatment.

Perfect agreement on claims C70-C76. Both evaluations explicitly affirm that ROCK inhibitor (Y-27632) reverses all protective effects of IL-1β in vivo, restoring SARS-CoV-2 spread in mouse lungs. Peer reviewers state this 'suggests that this inhibitory process functions in vivo' and confirms RhoA/ROCK pathway dependence.
